messages.subject: Re: Estimating Items Parameters With Known Thetas
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Items Parameters With Known Thetas
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pedro,

Unfortunately, no you won't be able to recover the most optimal item parameters given point estimates of the thetas, unfortunately, because the point estimates for each participant do not contain information pertaining to their complete sampling variability. Plus, each estimate has a certain degree of shrinkage/bias associated with the estimates, so even obtaining unbiased IRT parameter estimates is unlikely. This is the main problem with the JML estimation criteria too. See this thread <https://groups.google.com/g/mirt-package/c/k0CJrNf9-vc/m/BA9r7ayhBAAJ>.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: issues with fscores and mixedmirt
messages.body_plain:
It would be a combination of the fixef() function and the randef() function to combine the fixed, model implied components from the regression weights, and then using some estimate of the random effect to account for the sampling variability/measurement imprecision. If no fixed effects were included then all you would need is randef() as the latent traits do not have conditional expectations implied by the beta weights. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: MIRT modeling for multiple attempt questions
messages.subject_clean: MIRT modeling for multiple attempt questions
messages.body_plain:
You might be able to model such an approach as a (generalized) partial credit model, where the response numbers correspond to whether they got the item completely wrong (0), answered it on the second attempt (1), or the first attempt (2). Though it depends on the nature of what you're exactly trying to model (e.g., do you care about the repeated response behaviour itself, or is that really just a nuisance design dimension that should be accommodated?).

Phil

messages.subject: scores from out of sample data
messages.subject_clean: scores from out of sample data
messages.body_plain:
Let's suppose that I estimated IRT parameters with a sample data (i.e. training sample) and perhaps a another sample covdata (for formulas in mirt and/or fixed in mixedmirt). My question is:
- Is there an easy way to estimate fscores (i.e. thetas) from another sample data that is independent of the sample used to estimate the model parameters (i.e. testing sample). Correspondingly, if I use mixef and/or fixed in the case of scores for mixedmirt, can I also use the covdata information of that independent sample to get the theta scores?
I played around and modified the @Data info in the mod output and it seems to work for fscores. I just wonder if there is an easiest way to achieve estimated scores from an independent sample.
- Also, how can I change the scale for the thetas from the typical range [-6 6] to reflect let's say that the theta scores are samples from a normal distribution with a given mean mu and standard deviation s.
Thanks in advance,

messages.subject: Re: [ext] Re: SEM starting point mirtCAT
messages.body_plain:
Strange, I just tried your code with the following data generation and couldn't reproduce the issue. Could you modify the following until the error is reproducible?

#####
library(mirt)
library(mirtCAT)

a <- matrix(rlnorm(10,.2,.3))

# for the graded model, ensure that there is enough space between the intercepts,
# otherwise closer categories will not be selected often (minimum distance of 0.3 here)
diffs <- t(apply(matrix(runif(10*4, .3, 1), 20), 1, cumsum))
diffs <- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
d <- diffs + rnorm(10)

data <- simdata(a, d, 1000, itemtype = 'graded')

model='f =  1-10
CONSTRAIN = (1-10,a1)
'
mod1 <- mirt(data, model, itemtype = 'gpcm')

# generate pattern
set.seed(1)
Theta = matrix(sample(fscores(mod1, method = "EAP"), size = 1000))
pattern = generate_pattern(mod1, Theta = as.matrix(Theta))

# stopping rule
design = list(min_SEM = 0.2, min_items = 1, max_items = 7)

# CAT
result = mirtCAT(mo = mod1, method="EAP", criteria = "MI", start_item = 'MI',
                 local_pattern = pattern[2,], design = design, progress = TRUE)

#####

Phil

messages.subject: RMSE for Observations is High
messages.body_plain:
I am conducting simulation models on the GRM's ability to recreate observed data. I am using the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) as my index to see if the model recreates the data well. I am getting high RMSE values in my simulated data sets. I am not sure if this is normal for simulation data. I also calculate the RMSE of each parameter. The parameters are recovered well with a range of RMSE values of .07 to .09; and the model fits the data well ( i.e. CFI = .99, RMSEA = .016).  Below is the code I use to create the data and run the analyses.
set.seed(1234)
nitem = 15
sample.size = 1000
a <- as.matrix(round(rlnorm(nitem, meanlog = 0.3, sdlog = 0.2), 3), ncol=1)
diffs<- t(apply(matrix(runif(nitem*4, .3, 1), nitem), 1, cumsum))
diffs<- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
d <- diffs + rnorm(nitem)
ability <- as.matrix(round(rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1), 3), ncol=1)

####Simulate response data and estimate item parameters
dat<- simdata(a=a, d=d,N=sample.size, itemtype = 'graded', Theta = ability)

modelGRM <- mirt(data = dat, 1, itemtype = 'graded')
M2(modelGRM) ##CFI = .99, RMSEA = .008
####Extract estimated item parameters and compute bias and RMSE
newdata <- data.frame(round((grm_predict(mod = modelGRM,newdata = NULL)),0))
###Compute RMSE and RORME
dat_matrix<-dat
grm_matrix<-data.matrix(newdata)

parameters <-as.data.frame(coef(modelGRM, simplify = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)$items)
###Note for IRTrees etc instead of bias put AIC and BIC
bias.a<-round(mean(parameters[,1]-a), 3)
bias.d1<-round(mean(parameters[,2]-d[,1]), 3)
bias.d2<-round(mean(parameters[,3]-d[,2]), 3)
bias.d3<-round(mean(parameters[,4]-d[,3]), 3)
bias.d4<-round(mean(parameters[,5]-d[,4]), 3)
rmse.a<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,1]-a)^2)),3)
rmse.d1<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,2]-d[,1])^2)),3)
rmse.d2<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,3]-d[,2])^2)),3)
rmse.d3<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,4]-d[,3])^2)),3)
rmse.d4<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,5]-d[,4])^2)),3)
###RMSE of observed and expected items
rmseob<-sqrt(mean((dat_matrix-grm_matrix)^2))

results <- data.frame(sample.size=sample.size, nitem=nitem, AIC=modelGRM@Fit$AIC,
                     BIC = modelGRM@Fit$BIC, SABIC = modelGRM@Fit$SABIC,bias.a = bias.a, bias.d1=bias.d1, bias.d2=bias.d2,
                     bias.d3=bias.d3, bias.d4=bias.d4, rmse.a = rmse.a, rmse.d1 = rmse.d1, rmse.d2 = rmse.d2,
                     rmse.d3 = rmse.d3, rmse.d4 = rmse.d4, rmseob = rmseob);results
#####Results
  sample.size nitem      AIC      BIC    SABIC bias.a bias.d1 bias.d2 bias.d3 bias.d4 rmse.a
1        1000    15 36700.16 37068.24 36830.03  0.008   0.055   0.042   0.035   0.036  0.096
  rmse.d1 rmse.d2 rmse.d3 rmse.d4   rmseob
1   0.085   0.077   0.098   0.085 1.669411

I have tried playing around with theta values so that the theta mean is 0 and the sd is 2.5 or 3. This reduces the rmseob a bit but it is still around 1.4. I have used the grmpredict function that is below on other studies and had relatively good RMSE values (usually around .8 if the model fits well). I am wondering is the high RMSE observed values for the responses is because it is a simulation or if I am doing something wrong (i.e. creating poor thetas or alpha etc).
grm_predict <- function(mod, newdata = NULL, theta = NULL) {
  j <- extract.mirt(mod, "nitems")

  if (!is.null(newdata)) {
    observed <- newdata
    theta <- do.call("rbind", lapply(1:nrow(newdata), function(i)
      fscores(mod, method='MAP',response.pattern = newdata[i,],
              append_response.pattern = F)))
    theta <- theta[, -grep("SE_", colnames(theta)), drop = F]

  } else if (is.null(theta)) {
    observed <- extract.mirt(mod, "data")
    theta <- fscores(mod, method='MAP')
  }

  items <- lapply(1:j, function(i) extract.item(mod, item = i))
  pred <- sapply(1:j, function(i) expected.item(items[[i]], theta, min = 0))
  colnames(pred) <- colnames(newdata)
  return(pred)
}
Any help with this issue would be greatly appreciated.
-Gene

messages.subject: Re: Interesting plot shape - theta vs. SE - EAP estimation
messages.subject_clean: Interesting plot shape - theta vs. SE - EAP estimation
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, it's what I expected. Because the test is so long (500+ items) the precision of the thetas can be really small, so the course integration gride used to compute EAP estimates will miss the more minute differences between the associated estimates (basically, the numerical integration is too course given how tight each posterior function is, so you get this back-and-forth between the quadrature nodes). Model estimates don't suffer from this problem as they are based on the highest point + quadratic behaviour of the posterior only, and in this case I would certainly prefer them to EAPs.

In any event, to fix this in very long tests like this just increase the quadpts argument, like the following:

mirt_thetas0 <- as.data.frame(fscores(mirt_model, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = TRUE)) # original with 61 quadrature
mirt_thetas1 <- as.data.frame(fscores(mirt_model, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = TRUE, quadpts = 401)) # many more

layout(matrix(1:2, 1))
plot(mirt_thetas0)
plot(mirt_thetas1)

Also, you might want to consider increasing the quadrature number when estimating this model as well since it might improve the IRT estimate precision as well, leading to an even more precise model. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Every item has identical DIF statistics in bifactor model
messages.subject_clean: Every item has identical DIF statistics in bifactor model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe,

There's a strong to good chance that bifactor models don't work super well with DIF, largely because of their identification constraints to perform the numerical integration efficiently. I don't prevent such inputs, but just want to warn you that care must be taken with these models as they are slightly more constrained at the outset than one might prefer....

Anyway, in this particular case I don't think you want the 'drop' scheme, but rather the 'add' one. Drop is used when you have equality constraints set up across groups but want them removed to see if the model improves; 'add' is the converse, where the item's respective parameters are freely estimated across the groups but you now want to impose an equality constraint to see if the model gets worse. So, drop is looking to see if the model significantly improves (i.e., item has DIF), while add is looking to see if the model gets worse under the constraint (i.e., contains DIF...). A little confusing in the terminology, but both are sides of the same coin. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
That was a typo (I meant modal estimates, as in the highest point of some density function). And to answer your question about numerical integration it's really just a trial and error approach until the error is sufficiently small, or the solution stops improving.  E.g., if you increase the default quadrature from 61 to 101 and saw no difference in the final observed log-likelihood, there's not much being gained from the added numerical precision. Adaptive quadrature rules of course exist, which aim to minimize the integration error explicitly, but they are generally quite heavy computationally in the context of estimating IRT models for tests with a moderate number of items. HTH.

Phil

Model estimates don't suffer from this problem as they are based on the highest point + quadratic behaviour of the posterior only, and in this case I would certainly prefer them to EAPs.

messages.subject: Re: TIF Interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jose,

This is likely due to a few items having very high slope parameters (the a1's from coef(mod) ). It's unlikely that this output is reliable since large slopes tend to have large sampling variability, so you might want to consider placing a Bayesian prior on these values to deter this type of solution. HTH.

Phil

Nikos

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the information Phil! I had not thought to look at the SE of the model.

On Friday, June 4, 2021 at 3:41:46 PM UTC-4 rphilip....@gmail.com wrote:
> I'm not sure why you believe the RMSE estimates are too high, they match the observed SEs quite well. I have no clue what grm_predict() is doing as that's not a function that ships with mirt.
>
> Also, computations like bias and RMSE are readily available in the SimDesign package, which might also help with the general flow and readability of the simulation (not to mention other features). HTH.
>
> ###################
>
> library(mirt)
>
>
> set.seed(1234)
> nitem = 15
> sample.size = 1000
> a <- as.matrix(round(rlnorm(nitem, meanlog = 0.3, sdlog = 0.2), 3), ncol=1)
> diffs<- t(apply(matrix(runif(nitem*4, .3, 1), nitem), 1, cumsum))
> diffs<- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
> d <- diffs + rnorm(nitem)
> ability <- as.matrix(round(rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1), 3), ncol=1)
>
> ####Simulate response data and estimate item parameters
> dat<- simdata(a=a, d=d,N=sample.size, itemtype = 'graded', Theta = ability)
>
>
> modelGRM <- mirt(data = dat, 1, itemtype = 'graded', SE=TRUE)
> coef(modelGRM, printSE=TRUE)
>
> $Item_1

> par 1.068 0.250 -0.468 -1.366 -2.012
> SE  0.085 0.078  0.079  0.090  0.105

>
> .....
>
> $Item_15
>        a1    d1     d2     d3     d4
> par 1.538 0.059 -0.936 -1.367 -2.243
> SE  0.109 0.089  0.096  0.103  0.124
>
> $GroupPars
>     MEAN_1 COV_11
> par      0      1
> SE      NA     NA

>
> Phil
>
>
> On Fri, Jun 4, 2021 at 10:24 AM mos...@gmail.com <mos...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I am conducting simulation models on the GRM's ability to recreate observed data. I am using the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) as my index to see if the model recreates the data well. I am getting high RMSE values in my simulated data sets. I am not sure if this is normal for simulation data. I also calculate the RMSE of each parameter. The parameters are recovered well with a range of RMSE values of .07 to .09; and the model fits the data well ( i.e. CFI = .99, RMSEA = .016).  Below is the code I use to create the data and run the analyses.
> > set.seed(1234)
> > nitem = 15
> > sample.size = 1000
> > a <- as.matrix(round(rlnorm(nitem, meanlog = 0.3, sdlog = 0.2), 3), ncol=1)
> > diffs<- t(apply(matrix(runif(nitem*4, .3, 1), nitem), 1, cumsum))
> > diffs<- -(diffs - rowMeans(diffs))
> > d <- diffs + rnorm(nitem)
> > ability <- as.matrix(round(rnorm(sample.size, mean = 0, sd = 1), 3), ncol=1)
> >
> > ####Simulate response data and estimate item parameters
> > dat<- simdata(a=a, d=d,N=sample.size, itemtype = 'graded', Theta = ability)
> >
> >
> > modelGRM <- mirt(data = dat, 1, itemtype = 'graded')
> > M2(modelGRM) ##CFI = .99, RMSEA = .008
> > ####Extract estimated item parameters and compute bias and RMSE
> > newdata <- data.frame(round((grm_predict(mod = modelGRM,newdata = NULL)),0))
> > ###Compute RMSE and RORME
> > dat_matrix<-dat
> > grm_matrix<-data.matrix(newdata)
> >
> > parameters <-as.data.frame(coef(modelGRM, simplify = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)$items)
> > ###Note for IRTrees etc instead of bias put AIC and BIC
> > bias.a<-round(mean(parameters[,1]-a), 3)
> > bias.d1<-round(mean(parameters[,2]-d[,1]), 3)
> > bias.d2<-round(mean(parameters[,3]-d[,2]), 3)
> > bias.d3<-round(mean(parameters[,4]-d[,3]), 3)
> > bias.d4<-round(mean(parameters[,5]-d[,4]), 3)
> > rmse.a<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,1]-a)^2)),3)
> > rmse.d1<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,2]-d[,1])^2)),3)
> > rmse.d2<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,3]-d[,2])^2)),3)
> > rmse.d3<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,4]-d[,3])^2)),3)
> > rmse.d4<-round(sqrt(mean((parameters[,5]-d[,4])^2)),3)
> > ###RMSE of observed and expected items
> > rmseob<-sqrt(mean((dat_matrix-grm_matrix)^2))
> >
> > results <- data.frame(sample.size=sample.size, nitem=nitem, AIC=modelGRM@Fit$AIC,
> >                      BIC = modelGRM@Fit$BIC, SABIC = modelGRM@Fit$SABIC,bias.a = bias.a, bias.d1=bias.d1, bias.d2=bias.d2,
> >                      bias.d3=bias.d3, bias.d4=bias.d4, rmse.a = rmse.a, rmse.d1 = rmse.d1, rmse.d2 = rmse.d2,
> >                      rmse.d3 = rmse.d3, rmse.d4 = rmse.d4, rmseob = rmseob);results
> > #####Results
> >   sample.size nitem      AIC      BIC    SABIC bias.a bias.d1 bias.d2 bias.d3 bias.d4 rmse.a
> > 1        1000    15 36700.16 37068.24 36830.03  0.008   0.055   0.042   0.035   0.036  0.096
> >   rmse.d1 rmse.d2 rmse.d3 rmse.d4   rmseob
> > 1   0.085   0.077   0.098   0.085 1.669411
> >
> > I have tried playing around with theta values so that the theta mean is 0 and the sd is 2.5 or 3. This reduces the rmseob a bit but it is still around 1.4. I have used the grmpredict function that is below on other studies and had relatively good RMSE values (usually around .8 if the model fits well). I am wondering is the high RMSE observed values for the responses is because it is a simulation or if I am doing something wrong (i.e. creating poor thetas or alpha etc).
> > grm_predict <- function(mod, newdata = NULL, theta = NULL) {
> >   j <- extract.mirt(mod, "nitems")
> >
> >   if (!is.null(newdata)) {
> >     observed <- newdata
> >     theta <- do.call("rbind", lapply(1:nrow(newdata), function(i)
> >       fscores(mod, method='MAP',response.pattern = newdata[i,],
> >               append_response.pattern = F)))
> >     theta <- theta[, -grep("SE_", colnames(theta)), drop = F]
> >
> >   } else if (is.null(theta)) {
> >     observed <- extract.mirt(mod, "data")
> >     theta <- fscores(mod, method='MAP')
> >   }
> >
> >   items <- lapply(1:j, function(i) extract.item(mod, item = i))
> >   pred <- sapply(1:j, function(i) expected.item(items[[i]], theta, min = 0))
> >   colnames(pred) <- colnames(newdata)
> >   return(pred)
> > }
> > Any help with this issue would be greatly appreciated.
> > -Gene

messages.body_plain:
pars = 'values' returns the data.frame of starting values, not the final values after estimation. So unless the model converged instantly you would expect these to differ.

Phil

messages.subject: About "gpcmIRT"
messages.body_plain:
Hi phil

Using mirt I realize that there is a function called "gpcmIRT" that differs from "gpcm" and if there is any evidence of being better "graded" proposed by Samejima. I have a one-dimensional test with five items and five likert response alternatives. Performing a comparative analysis I observe that the gpcmIRT has a better fit in my data than the "graded" one. The question is when is it convenient to use "gpcmIRT"?

Best regards
Jose Ventura-Leon

messages.body_plain:
Given the magnitude of the parameters the models aren't numerically stable, so you shouldn't interpret them (the slopes are all effectively inf, and therefore all responses are effectively step-functions. Use plot(mirt_model, type = 'trace')) ). Plus, the amount of uncertainty in the model clearly indicates something has gone wrong:

messages.body_plain:
Thanks. The reason this happens is because the number of items in the test is quite large, so using rough numerical integration grids is likely the culprit. E.g., changing mirt's 61 to 151 you can see a small increase in the log-likelihood function, so there's precision to gain.

> mod <- mirt(responses, 1)
Iteration: 266, Log-Lik: -463630.528, Max-Change: 0.00009
> mod151 <- mirt(responses, 1, quadpts = 151)
Iteration: 500, Log-Lik: -462897.057, Max-Change: 0.00097

For ltm, I believe the package uses something quite small, like only 15 Gauss-Hermite quadrature nodes. Hence, it probably terminates much too early. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Thank you,

I checked ltm results with default mirt's number of quadrature points (61) and mirt results with default ltm's number of quadrature points (15). Here's what I got:

61 quadrature points (mirt's default)

ltm
ltm_model <- ltm(responses ~ z1, IRT.param = FALSE, control = list(GHk = 61))

summary(ltm_model)$logLik
## [1] -466025.8

ltm_params <- as.data.frame(coef(ltm_model))
head(ltm_params)
## (Intercept) z1
## item1 0.3814645 0.6275291
## item2 2.8976562 0.7364706
## item3 2.1075957 0.6449390

mirt

mirt_model <- mirt(responses, 1, SE=TRUE)

## Log-likelihood = -463630.5

mirt_params <- as.data.frame(coef(mirt_model, simplify = TRUE)$items)[1:2]
head(mirt_params)
## a1 d
## item1 0.9245075 0.3186796
## item2 1.0418570 2.8053719
## item3 0.9356348 2.0431438

15 quadrature points (ltm's default)

ltm
ltm_model <- ltm(responses ~ z1, IRT.param = FALSE)

summary(ltm_model)$logLik
## [1] -470030.7

ltm_params <- as.data.frame(coef(ltm_model))
head(ltm_params)
## (Intercept) z1
## item1 0.5007685 0.5062726
## item2 3.0325412 0.6000710
## item3 2.2231741 0.5203958

mirt
mirt_model <- mirt(responses, 1, SE=TRUE, quadpts = 15)
## Log-likelihood = -472591.2

mirt_params <- as.data.frame(coef(mirt_model, simplify = TRUE)$items)[1:2]
head(mirt_params)
## a1 d
## item1 0.4430672 0.460863
## item2 0.5269768 2.979918
## item3 0.4586273 2.183469

Shouldn't they give similar results with analogous number of quadrature points?

They'll only give similar results when increasing quadrature, not decreasing (mirt uses rectangular quadrature; ltm using GH).

Phil

messages.subject: Mixing numerical and categorical item responses with MIRT
messages.subject_clean: Mixing numerical and categorical item responses with MIRT
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I was wondering how to build a latent variable that takes into account both numerical and categorical item responses with MIRT.

https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/mirt/versions/1.33.2/topics/mirt

I am aware that we can mix item types by passing a vector to the itemtype argument of the MIRT function. What is the appropriate item type to use when one item has linear (or polynominal?)  relationship with the factor? An graded item type with infinite categories would do?

Looking forward to hearing from you,

Hugo

messages.subject_clean: Mixing numerical and categorical item responses with MIRT
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Do you think this would be a reasonable approach? Suppose I have three different types of items and I want to build a latent variable out of a combination of the three.

_OC - indicating ordinal categorical item
_NC - indicating nominal categorical item
_N   - indicating numerical item

First, I am thinking of creating a latent variable combining only categorical items using MIRT.

> y1 =f (I1_OC,I2_NC,I3_NC, I4_OC, I5_NC, etc.)

and then, creating a second latent variable combining my numerical items with y1 latent variable using lavaan or some other SEM software.

> y2 = f(I6_N, I7_N, y1)

Any concerns about this approach?

Looking forward to hearing from you,

Hugo

messages.subject: Re: P1-P4 in iteminfo (type = 'info')
messages.body_plain:
I hope that this is the right group to ask this question. Kindly inform me of the right group if my question is not appropriate here. This question is about the interpretation of IRT results rather than MIRT software in particular.

Intuitively, I thought that expected probably of endorsement for a particular category would be conceptually similar to (and associated with) the measurement accuracy for that particular category. If the expected probability is high for a particular category (within a specific theta range), then the items would be more sensitive (and thus providing more information) in measuring participants (within a specific theta range). I am fairly new in IRT, however, and thus my understanding of IRT can be naive.

Examples in the item trace lines:

For the items on the first row, the P3 (green) peaks are noticeably higher than the P2 (pink) peaks. Can I conclude that these items are particularly suitable (i.e., more sensitive) to measurement of people below average (around theta = -1 to +0.5) than people above average?  My hypothesis is that these items are more suitable for measuring participants at the relatively lower end of the trait.
Again, for items on the second row,  the P3 (green) peaks are noticeably higher than the P2 (pink) peaks.  Can I conclude that these items are particularly suitable (i.e., more sensitive) to measurement of people above average (around theta = 0 to +1.5) than people below average? My hypothesis is that these items are more suitable for measuring participants at the relatively higher end of the trait.

If my understanding is correct, then the item information curves below do not make sense to me. Items on the first row do not seem particularly good (i.e., provide more information?) in measuring people at the lower end of the trait (than people  at the higher end of the trait  ), and items on the second row do not seem particularly good (i.e.,  provide more information?) in measuring people  at the higher end of the trait  (than people at the lower end of the trait). The 'categories' all have the same peak.

Thanks again for your help!

Chester

messages.body_plain:
I don't think that the probability of endorsing a specific category is the same construct as the amount of information obtained. Information should be conceptually related to reliability and not to the result on the item. Furthermore, I think that the plots in the output show the information of the whole item, and not just specific categories.
